content: The outer packaging may include insulated vessels or flasks to facilitate the safe dissipation of carbon dioxide gas. Recycling of packaging materials is encouraged, and these materials can be returned or reused. However, before returning empty packaging to the consignor or sending it elsewhere, it must be disinfected or sterilized to eliminate any potential hazards. Additionally, any labels or markings indicating that the packaging previously contained infectious substances must be removed or obliterated. If packaging is reused, the shipper must ensure that all labels and markings accurately reflect the current contents being shipped, rather than the substances previously contained. Reused packaging must also retain its compliance with the quality testing standards outlined for Category A and Category B packaging requirements. Damaged or weakened packaging should no longer be used. Depending on the susceptibility of each biological agent, certain stabilizers may inactivate the agent, rendering it non-infectious to humans or animals. In such cases, professional judgment may be applied to reclassify the substance under the definition of an exemption. Once the appropriate packaging materials have been assembled, they must be clearly marked and labeled to provide information about the package's contents, the nature of the hazard, and the packaging standards applied. All marks and labels must be clearly visible and not obscured by other labels or markings. For infectious substances, the outer package must display the following marks: The shipper’s (sender’s or consignor’s) name and address. The receiver’s (consignee’s) name and address. The UN number of the infectious substance, followed by its proper shipping name. For substances requiring coolants (e.g., dry ice), the UN number and proper shipping name of the coolant must be provided, followed by the words AS COOLANT. The net quantity of the coolant present must also be indicated. For Category A infectious substances, the UN packaging symbol and certification marks must be displayed. If an overpack is used, these marks will not appear on the overpack. Additionally, the name and telephone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the shipment must be provided. The net quantity of dry ice is particularly important for shipment handling, as it determines how long a cool temperature can be maintained to preserve or stabilize the infectious substance during transit. In some cases, the dry ice may need to be replenished during transit to maintain the cold chain over a long journey. The net quantity of the infectious substance is also critical for biosafety and chain-of-custody purposes, as well as for assessing biosafety risks in the event of spillage or leakage. Hazard labels must be diamond-shaped, with minimum dimensions of 100 mm x 100 mm. If the package is small, the label size may be proportionally reduced, provided all elements remain visible. Each dangerous good in the package must have a corresponding hazard label unless specifically exempted. For Category A infectious substances, the hazard label must include: Three crescents superimposed on a black circle in the upper half of the diamond. The inscriptions INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE and In case of damage or leakage immediately notify Public Health Authority in black in the lower half. The number 6 displayed in the bottom corner. For packages containing dry ice as a coolant, a miscellaneous dangerous goods hazard label is required. This label must include seven vertical stripes in the upper portion and the number 9 underlined in the bottom corner. For liquid nitrogen or other compressed gases used as coolants, a non-flammable, non-toxic gas hazard label must be displayed. This label must include a gas cylinder symbol and the number 2 in the bottom corner. Handling labels, such as orientation arrows, are required for packages containing liquids to ensure they are handled in an upright position to prevent leakage. For infectious substances, orientation arrows are mandatory when primary receptacles exceed 50 mL. Packages containing infectious substances exceeding the quantity limits for passenger aircraft must display a Cargo Aircraft Only (CAO) label. This label must have minimum dimensions of 120 mm x 110 mm and an orange background with black writing. For cryogenic liquids like liquid nitrogen, an additional warning label must be used alongside the hazard label for non-flammable, non-toxic gases. This label may include the optional wording: Caution – may cause cold burn injuries if spilled or leaked. Transport documentation, such as the Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD), is required for all shipments of Category A infectious substances and certain medical or clinical wastes. However, Category B infectious substances assigned to UN 3373 and packaged according to Packing Instruction P650 are exempt from this requirement. The DGTD must include: 1. The name and address of the shipper (consignor) and receiver (consignee). 2. The name and contact phone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the infectious substance. 3. The date the document was signed. 4. A description of the dangerous goods, including the UN number, proper shipping name, technical name (if applicable), and any other required descriptive information. If a coolant like dry ice is present, it must be listed as a separate entry in the description. The type and quantity of packaging used, as well as any handling requirements, must also be specified. The shipper must provide a signed and dated certification statement acknowledging that the package has been prepared in compliance with applicable regulations. An air waybill is required for all shipments of infectious substances via international air transport, even if a DGTD is not required. This document must accompany the shipment and comply with the general conditions of carriage.
